analysis.one_liner: Makes it an unfair labor practice for employers to deny reinstatement to senior strikers after a strike ends.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 23 cosponsors, never left a House subcommittee and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, when a strike ends, an employer may keep the workers who crossed the picket line and leave out striking employees who had more seniority. This bill would make that refusal an unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act, forcing employers to reinstate their more senior employees once a strike is over. It applied to strikes beginning on or after January 1, 1990. The bill was introduced in June 1989, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Unionized workers who go on strike — especially long-tenured employees — would gain a legal guarantee that they get their jobs back when a strike ends, ahead of any replacements or strikebreakers the employer would rather keep. Unions would gain leverage in strikes because management could no longer simply wait out a walkout and staff the workplace permanently with replacement workers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new unfair labor practice: after a strike concludes, an employer may not fail to reinstate employees who have greater seniority than the employees who returned to work during the strike and whom the employer wants to keep [S2][S3].
Under then-existing law, an employer could retain replacement workers hired during a strike and leave senior strikers without their old jobs; this bill would close that gap for senior employees [S2].
It took effect for strikes commencing on or after January 1, 1990, so the protection would have applied to new disputes immediately [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing strikes would bear the cost: they could no longer permanently replace senior strikers with lower-priority workers, which would raise the cost of resisting a strike and could force layoffs of replacement hires once a strike ends. Businesses argued this shifts bargaining power toward unions and limits employer flexibility in staffing after a work stoppage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing strikes and their replacements

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose the ability to rebuild their workforce around the employees who kept working during a strike, forcing them to restore seniority-based staffing even after a long and costly walkout [S3].

A good-faith objection: making it an unfair labor practice to retain strikebreakers over senior strikers could escalate strikes, since management would face sharper consequences for outlasting a walkout — raising the stakes on both sides of a dispute [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For striking workers the gain is concrete and meaningful: a guaranteed path back to their jobs when a strike ends, protecting decades of accumulated seniority. The cost falls on employers, who would have less flexibility to retain replacement workers and would face stronger incentives to settle strikes quickly. The bill was narrowly drawn — it did not ban permanent replacements outright, only required that senior employees be reinstated over them — so the economic effect would have been modest outside active labor disputes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Russo of Illinois introduced the bill on June 13, 1989, joining with Rep. George Miller of California [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
On July 12, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, and no further action is recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 23 cosponsors — 22 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never reached the House floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who wanted to retain strikebreakers over senior strikers kept that ability, since the loophole the bill targeted remains open. The committee leadership that declined to act avoided a fight with business groups over labor law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; the bill died in subcommittee

for.name: Rep. Martin A. Russo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make refusing to reinstate senior strikers an unfair labor practice.

for.name: Rep. George Miller of California
for.what_they_did: Joined Russo in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

against.role: Chair and committee controlling the bill's calendar
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Labor-Management Relations subcommittee on July 12, 1989, and never scheduled a markup or floor action; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 22 of the 23 cosponsors were House Democrats, with one Republican; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Unionized employers (manufacturing, transportation, and other strike-prone industries)
industries.note: The bill would have barred these employers from keeping replacement workers over senior strikers after a strike, raising the cost of resisting walkouts. The bill died, so their existing ability to retain strikebreakers was preserved.

The bill would have strengthened unions' hand in strikes by guaranteeing senior members their jobs back, making a walkout a more credible threat. Union members are the workers the bill protects directly.
